claims.evidence: NHS warfarin service: INR is a standard test of clotting time used to check how strongly warfarin is affecting you; dosing advice based on latest INR.
INR stands for International Normalised Ratio.
Standard test of clotting time.
Rotherham leaflet: INR compares clotting time on warfarin with clotting time off it.
'There is no fixed dose'; no standard dose for warfarin.
Dose adjusts depending on INR reading; INR checks how strongly warfarin is acting.
Bleeding named as the biggest risk; 'highest when INR too high' was not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding.

claims.evidence: NHS: when first starting, tests may be needed every day or every few days.
Once stable, tests lengthen (weekly to 12 weekly depending on results).
NHS: some people need tests more often.
Dosing advice is based on the latest INR result; blood test interval depends on INR results.
NHS service advises an INR test 5-7 days after starting or stopping any new medicine.
Vitamin K intake changes affect INR; binge drinking can raise INR; tell clinic about other medicines.
NHS trust: avoid cranberry and grapefruit juice because they raise bleeding risk; binge drinking can raise INR. 'Raise the INR' not stated for juices.
claims.newSentence: Sources name cranberry and grapefruit juice as drinks to avoid on warfarin, and binge drinking as able to raise the INR.

claims.evidence: Children's NHS leaflet: ibuprofen-type NSAIDs can increase bleeding; NHS says avoid ibuprofen, use paracetamol.
GOSH list: cut not stopping after 5-10 min pressure, blood in urine, coffee-ground or red vomit, red or black stools; bleeding gums in other leaflets.
CUH: heavier periods are a reason to contact GP or 111 (other leaflet says some increase can be expected; sources differ).
'The NHS says' (nhs.uk page) was not confirmed. CUH leaflet: minor bruising or bleeding, consult GP or NHS 111.
claims.newSentence: NHS trust leaflets say to contact the GP or NHS 111 about minor bruising or bleeding.

claims.evidence: BHF page text was not returned. Several NHS leaflets say call 999 if bleeding cannot be stopped.
claims.newSentence: NHS leaflets say to call 999 if bleeding cannot be stopped.

claims.evidence: NHS inform page not returned. CUH and GOSH list vomiting or coughing up blood as needing A&E/urgent care.
claims.newSentence: NHS trust leaflets list vomiting or coughing up blood as a reason to seek care at A&E.

claims.evidence: NBT: seek urgent medical attention (999) for a significant blow to the head. 'Even without visible bleeding' not stated.
claims.newSentence: NHS guidance says a significant blow to the head is a reason to call 999.

claims.evidence: Rotherham: new patients are given an Alert Card.
Hospital leaflet: card important if in an accident, lets staff identify that you take warfarin.
Vitamin K foods (broccoli, cabbage, leafy greens) affect how warfarin works.
Do not need to avoid them, eat consistent amounts; clinic can adjust dose.
NHS: food and drink restrictions do not usually apply to apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban. Ledger URL was /conditions/anticoagulants/; correct is /medicines/.
INR is a clotting-time test used to check warfarin effect.
No fixed dose; dose adjusts to INR reading.
Diet (vitamin K), binge drinking and new medicines affect INR.
'The NHS says 111' on nhs.uk not confirmed; NHS trust leaflets give GP/111 for minor bleeding and 999 when bleeding cannot be stopped.
claims.newSentence: The main side effect of warfarin is bleeding; NHS leaflets advise a GP or NHS 111 for minor bleeding and 999 if it will not stop.

additions.sentence: One NHS trust explains that an INR of 2.0 means the blood takes roughly twice as long to clot as it would without warfarin.
additions.evidence: INR of 2.0 means blood takes roughly twice as long to clot on warfarin.

additions.sentence: The target INR depends on the reason for treatment, and the consultant sets the exact target.
additions.evidence: Target ranges depend on the reason for treatment; consultant sets exact target.

additions.sentence: One NHS trust says that once the INR is stable, the gap between blood tests can lengthen to as much as 8 to 12 weeks.
additions.evidence: Once stabilised the time between blood tests lengthens to a maximum of 8-12 weeks.

additions.sentence: The NHS advises telling the GP, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter or herbal medicine, including aspirin and St John's wort.
additions.evidence: Tell your GP, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist about any prescription, OTC or herbal medicine, including aspirin and St John's Wort.

additions.sentence: NHS advice is that people taking warfarin should never binge drink.
additions.evidence: Do not binge drink while taking warfarin.

additions.sentence: The NHS says the anticoagulant alert card should be carried at all times and shown to a doctor or dentist before any procedure.
additions.evidence: Always carry this with you. Show it to your doctor or dentist before procedures.

additions.sentence: A sudden change in the amount of vitamin K in the diet can change how much warfarin a person needs.
additions.evidence: A sudden change in vitamin K intake can shift warfarin needs.

notes: Author URL for NHS anticoagulants page was /conditions/anticoagulants/considerations/; correct is /medicines/anticoagulants/considerations/. BHF and NHS inform warfarin pages and the nhs.uk warfarin 111 wording were not returned in text, so c19, c20, c18, c30 were reworded to NHS trust leaflets. Sources differ on whether heavier periods are urgent (c17).
